narration_line: On a calm spring afternoon in 1915, a single torpedo struck the most famous liner on the Atlantic.
visual: the four-funnelled liner Lusitania steaming on a calm sea, a thin white torpedo wake approaching her starboard side
camera_move: slow push-in as the wake streaks toward the hull

narration_line: Eighteen minutes later, she was gone, and nearly twelve hundred people had died with her.
visual: Lusitania's stern rising above the sea, tiny lifeboats and debris around her, smoke over the water
camera_move: slow pull-out as the stern sinks lower

narration_line: One hundred and twenty-eight of the dead were citizens of a country not even at war.
visual: a neat row of small paper American passports and luggage tags on a wooden desk, one tag reading "New York"
camera_move: slow lateral pan along the row

narration_line: Here's how the sinking of the Lusitania turned America against Germany.
visual: relief map of the Atlantic, a dotted route from New York to Ireland ending in a small red cross off the Irish coast
camera_move: gentle tilt down onto the red cross

narration_line: And why it still took two more years before American soldiers went to war.
visual: rows of American doughboy soldiers in 1917 olive uniforms and brimmed helmets marching toward a troopship
camera_move: slow parallax pan with the column

narration_line: When war broke out in Europe in August 1914, the United States chose to stay out.
visual: relief map of Europe with raised red front lines across France, the United States shown separately across the ocean in calm green
camera_move: slow pull-out from Europe to reveal America

narration_line: President Woodrow Wilson asked Americans to be neutral in thought as well as action.
visual: Woodrow Wilson seated at his desk signing a document, a small American flag on the desk

narration_line: Millions of Americans had roots in Germany, Ireland and Britain, and few wanted another country's war.
visual: a busy 1914 New York street of paper-cut townhouses, shopfronts and families in period clothing
camera_move: lateral parallax pan along the street

narration_line: Yet American factories and banks were already trading heavily with Britain and France.
visual: a 1915 American factory yard with smoking chimneys and crates being loaded onto a cargo ship
camera_move: slow pan across the crates to the ship

narration_line: Britain's navy blockaded Germany, choking the flow of food and raw materials to its ports.
visual: relief map of the North Sea with a chain of small grey British warship tokens forming a line across it
camera_move: tokens slide into a closed line

narration_line: Germany answered with a new kind of weapon that struck from beneath the waves.
visual: the grey German submarine U-20 surfacing in a choppy sea, water streaming from its deck
camera_move: slow push-in as the submarine rises

narration_line: In February 1915, Germany declared the waters around Britain a war zone.
visual: a 1915 German government proclamation on aged paper with an eagle seal, headline reading "War Zone"

narration_line: Enemy merchant ships in that zone could now be sunk without warning, and neutrals sailed at risk.
visual: relief map of the British Isles ringed by a dashed red boundary line in the sea
camera_move: the red boundary draws itself around the islands

narration_line: Wilson replied that Germany would be held to strict accountability for any American lives lost.
visual: Woodrow Wilson standing at his desk holding a letter, looking down at it with a stern expression

narration_line: In March, an American named Leon Thrasher drowned when a U-boat sank the British ship Falaba.
visual: a lone man in a 1915 suit and lifejacket on the deck of a small sinking steamer, grey sea around

narration_line: Then, on May 1, a U-boat torpedoed the American tanker Gulflight, and three men died.
visual: a low black oil tanker with a striped American flag painted on its hull, smoke from a hole in its bow

narration_line: At the centre of this danger sailed the Lusitania, pride of the Cunard line.
visual: Lusitania at a New York pier, four tall red and black funnels, crowds of passengers on the dock
camera_move: slow upward tilt along the funnels

narration_line: When she entered service in 1907, she was one of the largest and fastest ships ever built.
visual: relief map of the North Atlantic with a liner token racing between Liverpool and New York, a small blue ribbon pinned beside it

narration_line: Her passengers included millionaires, families, nannies and children, all bound for Liverpool.
visual: passengers in 1915 clothing on the liner's deck: a wealthy man in a top hat, a mother with two children, a nanny

narration_line: On the morning she sailed, a strange notice appeared in American newspapers.
visual: a 1915 man in a bowler hat at a breakfast table frowning at his folded newspaper

narration_line: The German embassy warned that travellers on British ships sailed at their own risk.
visual: close-up of a boxed newspaper notice with a heavy black border, headline reading "Notice"

narration_line: In some papers, it was printed right beside Cunard's advertisement for the Lusitania.
visual: a newspaper page showing two boxed notices side by side, one with a small ship drawing
camera_move: slow lateral pan from one box to the other

narration_line: Almost nobody cancelled, because no one believed Germany would sink a ship full of civilians.
visual: crowds of passengers walking up the gangway onto the Lusitania, porters carrying trunks
camera_move: slow pan following the crowd up the gangway

narration_line: On May 1, 1915, the Lusitania left New York with nearly two thousand people aboard.
visual: Lusitania pulling away from the New York pier, tugboats beside her, the skyline behind
camera_move: slow pull-out as the ship departs

narration_line: Commanding her was Captain William Turner, one of Cunard's most experienced captains.
visual: Captain William Turner on the ship's bridge in a dark naval-style captain's uniform and cap, looking out to sea

narration_line: To save coal, one of her four boiler rooms had been shut down, cutting her top speed.
visual: a ship's boiler room with three glowing furnaces and one dark cold furnace, stokers with shovels
camera_move: slow pan from the glowing furnaces to the dark one

narration_line: Meanwhile, off the south coast of Ireland, a German submarine was hunting.
visual: U-20 cruising low in a grey misty sea, the dark Irish coastline faint behind

narration_line: The liner was just eleven miles off the Irish coast, almost within sight of safety.
visual: relief map of southern Ireland with a small liner token near the Old Head of Kinsale and a submarine token nearby
camera_move: slow push-in on the two tokens

narration_line: U-20 was commanded by Walther Schwieger, a young officer who had already sunk several ships that week.
visual: Walther Schwieger in a dark German naval officer's uniform and cap in a cramped submarine control room

narration_line: On May 7, Turner slowed his ship in thick fog as he neared the Old Head of Kinsale.
visual: Lusitania emerging from lifting fog near tall green Irish headland cliffs with a small lighthouse

narration_line: Through his periscope, Schwieger saw four funnels rising above the horizon.
visual: view through a round periscope lens: the four funnels of a distant liner on the horizon

narration_line: At ten minutes past two in the afternoon, he fired a single torpedo.
visual: Walther Schwieger at the periscope in the dim control room, raising one hand to give the firing order

narration_line: It struck the starboard side, just behind the bridge.
visual: a tall white water column and orange flash erupting against the liner's starboard side near the front

narration_line: Seconds later, a second, much larger explosion tore through the ship from inside.
visual: a second burst of smoke and orange light erupting from the hull, debris flying

narration_line: In his war diary, Schwieger noted an unusually heavy explosion and a huge cloud of smoke.
visual: an open German naval logbook with handwritten entries and a pen, inside a dim submarine

narration_line: Historians still argue about that second blast, from boilers and steam to coal dust or cargo.
visual: a historian's desk with a cutaway paper diagram of a liner's hull and three question marks in pencil

narration_line: The Lusitania lurched hard to starboard, and water poured into her open portholes.
visual: the liner listing steeply to one side, sea washing over the lower decks

narration_line: Her steep tilt made most lifeboats impossible to lower safely.
visual: lifeboats swinging out awkwardly from their davits on a tilted deck, crew struggling with ropes
camera_move: slow lateral pan along the boats

narration_line: Of her forty-eight lifeboats, only six were successfully lowered.
visual: a deck plan of a liner on paper showing 48 small lifeboat shapes, only six coloured in

narration_line: Passengers jumped into the cold water, clinging to deck chairs, oars and wreckage.
visual: people in lifejackets floating among wooden deck chairs and debris on the sea, no injuries shown

narration_line: Just eighteen minutes after the torpedo struck, the great ship slipped beneath the sea.
visual: the last of the liner's stern vanishing into the sea, a swirl of water and smoke

narration_line: Schwieger did not stay to help, and U-20 slipped away toward home.
visual: Walther Schwieger lowering the periscope handles, turning away with a hard expression

narration_line: Fishing boats and steamers rushed from the coast to pull survivors from the water.
visual: small fishing boats and a steamer arriving among floating debris, sailors reaching down to people

narration_line: Survivors and the dead were brought to the Irish port of Queenstown.
visual: a small Irish harbour town at dusk, terraced houses and a cathedral above the quay, boats arriving

narration_line: Nearly twelve hundred people were lost, including ninety-four children.
visual: a quiet memorial table with rows of small white candles and a single child's shoe

narration_line: Within hours, the news flashed across the Atlantic by telegraph.
visual: a 1915 telegraph operator in sleeve garters and an eyeshade tapping a brass telegraph key

narration_line: American newspapers filled their front pages with the names of the dead.
visual: a stack of 1915 American newspapers with huge headlines reading "Lusitania Sunk"

narration_line: Among them were famous Americans, like the millionaire Alfred Vanderbilt and the producer Charles Frohman.
visual: two well-dressed 1915 gentlemen in paper-cut portrait frames on a mantelpiece, one in a bowler hat
camera_move: slow lateral pan between the frames

narration_line: Of the one hundred and fifty-nine Americans aboard, one hundred and twenty-eight never came home.
visual: a passenger list on a desk with many names crossed through in ink

narration_line: Crowds gathered outside newspaper offices in New York, waiting for each new list of names.
visual: a crowd in 1915 hats and coats outside a newspaper office with a bulletin board

narration_line: Former president Theodore Roosevelt called the attack piracy and demanded action.
visual: Theodore Roosevelt with round spectacles and a thick moustache, speaking forcefully at a lectern with a raised fist

narration_line: Editorials called it murder on the high seas and a crime against civilisation.
visual: an open newspaper editorial page with a dark cartoon of a submarine and a sinking ship

narration_line: Germany insisted that the Lusitania was a legitimate target carrying weapons for Britain.
visual: a German diplomat in a dark frock coat reading a statement to reporters with notepads

narration_line: Berlin even claimed the ship was armed, but American inspectors had found no guns aboard.
visual: an American port inspector in a 1915 suit with a clipboard on an empty liner deck, no guns anywhere

narration_line: Her cargo did include millions of rifle cartridges and over a thousand cases of shrapnel shells.
visual: wooden crates stamped with simple markings in a ship's hold, a few brass rifle cartridges spilling from one

narration_line: But to most Americans, that could never justify drowning women and children without warning.
visual: a mother and child in lifejackets on a tilted deck, holding hands, looking toward a lifeboat

narration_line: For the first time, many ordinary Americans saw Germany not as a distant power, but as a threat.
visual: an American family in a 1915 parlour reading a newspaper together with worried faces

narration_line: Woodrow Wilson now faced the hardest choice of his presidency.
visual: Woodrow Wilson standing alone at a tall window at night, hands behind his back, lamp light behind him

narration_line: Three days later, he told a Philadelphia audience that a nation could be too proud to fight.
visual: Woodrow Wilson speaking from a stage draped with red, white and blue bunting to a seated audience

narration_line: The phrase was mocked by critics, who saw it as weakness in the face of murder.
visual: a newspaper cartoon on a desk showing a small figure hiding behind a large book labelled "Notes"

narration_line: Instead of war, Wilson sent Germany a series of sharp diplomatic notes.
visual: Woodrow Wilson typing a letter on his own typewriter at his desk, lamp light

narration_line: The first, in May, demanded that Germany stop attacking unarmed passenger ships.
visual: a single typed letter being slipped into an envelope stamped "Berlin"

narration_line: His Secretary of State, William Jennings Bryan, feared the notes would drag America into war.
visual: William Jennings Bryan, a broad balding man in a dark frock coat, frowning over papers at a desk

narration_line: America's ambassador in London warned that the country must declare war or lose Europe's respect.
visual: a 1915 American diplomat writing a letter at a desk in a London embassy office, rain on the window

narration_line: On June 9, rather than sign the second note, Bryan resigned.
visual: a handwritten resignation letter on a desk beside a fountain pen and an inkwell

narration_line: His replacement, Robert Lansing, was far more sympathetic to Britain.
visual: Robert Lansing, a neat grey-haired man with a moustache, standing beside a globe

narration_line: A third note in July warned that further attacks would be seen as deliberately unfriendly.
visual: a typed diplomatic note with a stern underlined final sentence, an inkwell beside it
camera_move: slow push-in on the underlined line

narration_line: Germany's replies defended the sinking and refused to admit it had been illegal.
visual: a German reply letter with an eagle seal lying on top of Wilson's own notes

narration_line: Wilson was walking a tightrope between public anger and his promise to keep America at peace.
visual: Woodrow Wilson at his desk between two stacks of letters, one tall and one short, looking at both

narration_line: Britain understood the power of the tragedy, and quickly turned it into a weapon.
visual: a busy British propaganda office with clerks at desks and a printing press producing posters

narration_line: In Germany, an artist named Karl Goetz made a satirical medal mocking the sinking.
visual: a dark bronze medal on a cloth, embossed with a sinking ship, under lamp light

narration_line: British officials made huge numbers of copies and sold them as proof of German cruelty.
visual: a busy 1915 London shop counter, customers buying small boxed medals from a clerk
camera_move: slow lateral pan along the case

narration_line: Days after the sinking, Britain also published the Bryce Report on German atrocities in Belgium.
visual: a thick bound government report on a desk, its cover reading "Report", with an official seal

narration_line: Many of its stories were later shown to be exaggerated, but in 1915 they were widely believed.
visual: 1915 readers in a library reading copies of the report with shocked faces

narration_line: In America, a famous recruiting poster showed a drowning mother clutching her baby beneath one word: Enlist.
visual: a framed 1915 poster on a brick wall showing a mother and baby sinking in green water, the single word "Enlist"

narration_line: The Lusitania became a symbol of a war being fought not just by armies, but against civilians.
visual: a man and a young boy in 1915 clothes stopping in front of the poster on a brick wall

narration_line: Anger over the sinking also boosted a Preparedness Movement demanding a bigger American army.
visual: a 1915 American rally with banners and a speaker on a platform before a crowd

narration_line: That summer, volunteers began training as officers at a camp in Plattsburgh, New York.
visual: rows of men in khaki drilling with rifles at a summer training camp beside a lake and pine trees

narration_line: In Berlin, German leaders realised they could not afford to push America any further.
visual: German officials in dark uniforms and frock coats around a long table in a Berlin ministry
camera_move: slow lateral pan around the table

narration_line: Germany's admirals were furious, convinced their submarines could win the war if they were unleashed.
visual: a German admiral in a dark naval uniform pounding a table beside a submarine model

narration_line: But in August 1915, another U-boat sank the British liner Arabic, and more Americans died.
visual: a two-funnelled liner listing after an explosion on a grey sea, smoke rising

narration_line: Facing a break with Washington, Germany promised not to sink passenger liners without warning.
visual: a German diplomatic letter with an eagle seal, a fountain pen signing at the bottom

narration_line: In March 1916, a torpedo hit the French ferry Sussex, injuring several Americans aboard.
visual: a small French cross-channel ferry with its bow blown away, still afloat on a grey sea

narration_line: Wilson threatened to cut diplomatic ties, and Germany promised again to restrain its submarines.
visual: Woodrow Wilson at his desk pointing firmly at a document, a German envoy standing opposite

narration_line: For the rest of 1916, the U-boats held back, and America stayed out of the war.
visual: a calm harbour with a submarine moored at a quay, its crew idle on deck

narration_line: In 1916, Wilson won re-election with a simple slogan: He kept us out of war.
visual: a 1916 campaign banner and badges on a table, the banner reading "He Kept Us Out of War"

narration_line: Yet beneath that peace, American trade, loans and sympathy were flowing steadily toward Britain.
visual: cargo ships loading at an American port, a line of ships heading east across the sea

narration_line: By early 1917, Germany's generals believed they could starve Britain before America could act.
visual: German generals with spiked helmets beside them leaning over a war-table map of the Atlantic

narration_line: On February 1, Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare across the Atlantic.
visual: relief map of the Atlantic with many small dark submarine tokens spreading out from Germany
camera_move: tokens slide outward across the ocean

narration_line: Germany knew this would probably bring America in, and gambled that it would not matter.
visual: Kaiser-era German officials around a war table, one pushing a submarine token toward America

narration_line: Two days later, Wilson broke off diplomatic relations with Germany.
visual: Woodrow Wilson handing a sealed envelope to an aide, a stern expression on his face

narration_line: Then British codebreakers revealed a secret German message called the Zimmermann Telegram.
visual: a decoded telegram on a desk with columns of numbers and pencilled words, a magnifying glass on it

narration_line: It offered Mexico Texas, New Mexico and Arizona if it joined a war against the United States.
visual: relief map of the southern United States and Mexico, the three states highlighted with a bold arrow from Mexico

narration_line: When the telegram was published on March 1, Americans were outraged.
visual: a 1917 American newspaper with a bold headline reading "Plot Exposed"

narration_line: In March, U-boats sank several American merchant ships, and public patience finally ran out.
visual: an American merchant ship with a flag painted on its side sinking in a grey sea

narration_line: On April 2, 1917, Wilson asked Congress for a declaration of war against Germany.
visual: Woodrow Wilson at a lectern before a packed Congress chamber, members standing

narration_line: He told them the world must be made safe for democracy.
visual: Woodrow Wilson at the lectern raising one hand, members of Congress applauding

narration_line: Four days later, on April 6, Congress voted for war.
visual: a 1917 newspaper on a desk with a huge headline reading "War Declared"

narration_line: As American soldiers sailed for France, the memory of the Lusitania sailed with them.
visual: American doughboys crowding a troopship deck, waving hats as it leaves harbour

narration_line: The Lusitania did not take America to war on its own.
visual: relief map of the Atlantic with the dotted Lusitania route and a small red cross off Ireland

narration_line: That took two years, broken promises, a secret telegram and more ships at the bottom of the sea.
visual: the same map now crowded with small sunken-ship tokens and a folded telegram lying on it

narration_line: But it was the moment millions of Americans first saw Germany as an enemy.
visual: an American family in their parlour, the father lowering a newspaper with a grave look

narration_line: In 1925, Germany finally paid compensation to the families of American victims.
visual: a signed legal document and a cheque-like paper on a desk with a 1925 date

narration_line: Today, the wreck still lies on the seabed off the Irish coast, a hundred metres below the waves.
visual: the dark wreck of the liner lying on its side on the seabed, fish around it, faint light from above

narration_line: The Lusitania did not drag America into the war, but it decided which side America would fight on.
visual: green Irish cliffs and the Old Head of Kinsale lighthouse at sunset, a calm golden sea where the ship was lost
camera_move: slow pull-out to a wide view
